passage: In the 1960s, the British psychologist Richard Gregory developed a classic demonstration of how expectations shape perception, using a hollow mask of a human face. When people look at the hollow inside of the mask from a short distance, they do not see a concave surface curving inward; instead, they perceive a normal, three-dimensional face bulging outward. Even when viewers know the mask is hollow and move their heads from side to side, the illusion persists, making the face appear to turn and follow them. Gregory explained that our brains rely heavily on prior knowledge and expectations to interpret ambiguous sensory data. Because we have spent our entire lives seeing convex faces rather than hollow ones, the brain overrides the actual visual cues from shadows and depth to impose the familiar pattern of a protruding face. This hollow-face illusion vividly shows that perception is not a passive recording of reality, but an active construction guided by what we expect to see.
